title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
An AI system was used to create a fake news article impersonating a real interview between a Reserve Bank Governor and a known finance presenter, designed to promote an unlicensed cryptocurrency platform. The fabricated content falsely attributed statements to real people to lend credibility to a fraudulent investment scheme. This deployment bypassed any verification step that might have checked whether the quoted individuals had actually made those statements or participated in the interview.

The scam exploited AI's ability to generate realistic-seeming text and the speed at which fabricated content spreads online before fact-checking occurs. Detection would have required either human review of the article before publication, verification of the interview's authenticity by platforms hosting it, or checks by the cryptocurrency platform itself against the sources it was using for promotion.

It is not established whether the AI system was purpose-built for fraud or a general text-generation tool repurposed by bad actors. The Australian Securities and Investments Commission reports a broader trend of AI-enabled impersonation and investment scams, though the specific technical details of how each scam operates remain unclear.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
# Summary

A fake online article falsely depicted Reserve Bank Governor Michele Bullock in a heated interview with ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler about an unlicensed cryptocurrency platform called Boulder Sparhaven. The interview never occurred, but the fabricated article was designed to promote the fraudulent investment scheme. This type of scam, using artificial intelligence to create deepfake content featuring well-known Australians, is becoming increasingly prevalent and sophisticated according to the Australian Securities and Investments Commission.

ASIC's research reveals that investment scams have risen dramatically, with the regulator removing 19,400 scams last year, a 182 percent increase. Phishing scams jumped 279 percent, while fake investment platforms increased by 151 percent. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is the most commonly impersonated public figure, followed by other politicians and business leaders including Alan Kohler, who has experienced similar scams before. The regulator warns consumers to verify licenses independently and avoid investments promoted through suspicious online content, while Kohler argues that platforms hosting such material should face substantial fines.
